factors.name: Doing vs. allowing
factors.description: Whether a person actively brings about an outcome or merely allows it when they could have prevented it; outcome, knowledge, motive and ease of acting otherwise are held fixed.

factors.name: Norm violation and causal judgment
factors.description: Whether a person's contribution to an outcome broke a rule or was permitted, with the physical contribution held fixed; the judgment is how much that person caused the outcome.

factors.name: Avoidable vs. unavoidable harm
factors.description: Whether a harm that follows a person's action would not have happened had they acted otherwise, or would have happened anyway; the action, what the person knows and wants, and the harm are held fixed.

factors.name: Knowing the rule, in causal judgment
factors.description: Whether a person who broke a rule, and whose action helped bring about an outcome, knew about the rule; the action, the rule, the outcome and others' contributions are held fixed; the judgment is how much that person caused the outcome.

factors.name: Moral luck in wrongness
factors.description: Whether one and the same choice, made with the same knowledge and risk, turns out harmlessly or harmfully; the judgment is how wrong the choice was, not blame or punishment.

factors.name: Null control
factors.description: An incidental detail that should not matter (control pairs only).

On Sunday, Daniel was walking the path alone. As he came up to the gate he read the sign and saw about thirty sheep grazing nearby. The gate was shut. He unlatched it, swung it wide open, walked through, and carried on, leaving it wide open behind him. He knew the sheep could get out. Shutting the gate would have taken him a few seconds, but he did not want to bother. Nobody else used the path that day. An hour later the sheep had wandered through the gate onto a nearby road. The farmer spent the whole afternoon rounding them up, and one sheep was hit by a car and killed.

B.text: A public footpath crosses a sheep farm. Where the path leaves the field there is a metal gate with a sign: 'Sheep in field. Walkers must shut this gate behind them.' On Sunday, Daniel was walking the path alone. As he came up to the gate he read the sign and saw about thirty sheep grazing nearby. The gate was already wide open; the wind had blown it open. He walked through and carried on, leaving it wide open behind him. He knew the sheep could get out. Shutting the gate would have taken him a few seconds, but he did not want to bother. Nobody else used the path that day. An hour later the sheep had wandered through the gate onto a nearby road. The farmer spent the whole afternoon rounding them up, and one sheep was hit by a car and killed.

judgment_question.text: How much blame does Daniel deserve for what happened to the sheep?

comprehension_question.text: According to the scenario, what state was the gate in when Daniel came up to it?

options.b: It was already wide open

pairs.intended_difference: In A Daniel himself opens the shut gate and leaves it open; in B the wind has already blown the gate open and he merely fails to shut it.

prediction.rationale: His knowledge, motive, the sign's instruction and the few-second cost are the same in both versions, so the failure to shut the gate will still draw heavy blame. I expect about one point more when he opened it himself (about 6.3 versus 5.2).

pairs.originality_note: Not a rescue or sacrifice dilemma: an everyday farm-gate case in which the allowing version has a non-human cause (wind), so no second wrongdoer absorbs the blame.

pairs.title: Storage shelf

A.text: The storage room of a community centre has one long wooden shelf, used for boxes. A notice fixed to the shelf says: 'For the choir only.' On Monday, Tessa, who belongs to the chess club, put a box of chess clocks on the shelf. The same day, Henrik, who belongs to the choir, put a box of songbooks on the shelf. Each box weighed twenty kilograms. The shelf was strong enough to hold either box by itself, but not both together. Neither Tessa nor Henrik knew this. During the night the shelf gave way under the weight of the two boxes and fell onto a table below, smashing a set of ceramic bowls made by the pottery class.

B.text: The storage room of a community centre has one long wooden shelf, used for boxes. A notice fixed to the shelf says: 'For the choir and the chess club.' On Monday, Tessa, who belongs to the chess club, put a box of chess clocks on the shelf. The same day, Henrik, who belongs to the choir, put a box of songbooks on the shelf. Each box weighed twenty kilograms. The shelf was strong enough to hold either box by itself, but not both together. Neither Tessa nor Henrik knew this. During the night the shelf gave way under the weight of the two boxes and fell onto a table below, smashing a set of ceramic bowls made by the pottery class.

judgment_question.text: How much did Tessa cause the shelf to collapse?

comprehension_question.text: According to the notice in the scenario, who was the shelf for?

options.b: The choir and the chess club

pairs.intended_difference: The notice on the shelf says 'For the choir only' in A, so Tessa's box was not allowed there, and 'For the choir and the chess club' in B, so it was allowed; nothing else changes.

prediction.rationale: With equal weights, readers will give an even-share answer near 4 when both boxes were allowed and move about one point up when Tessa's box was not supposed to be there. Some readers will hold to the physical half-share, which should keep the gap below 1.5.

pairs.title: The house dressing

A.text: Dan, the best player at his tennis club, has reached the final of a tournament against a much stronger visiting player. Dan knows that his opponent is allergic to cayenne pepper and that the club restaurant's house dressing contains cayenne. The night before the match, the two have dinner at the club. Dan hopes his opponent will eat the house dressing, get a stomach ache, and play badly. His opponent is about to order the Italian dressing when Dan recommends the house dressing instead, and his opponent orders it. His opponent eats the salad, gets a stomach ache that night, and loses the final to Dan the next day.

B.text: Dan, the best player at his tennis club, has reached the final of a tournament against a much stronger visiting player. Dan knows that his opponent is allergic to cayenne pepper and that the club restaurant's house dressing contains cayenne. The night before the match, the two have dinner at the club. Dan hopes his opponent will eat the house dressing, get a stomach ache, and play badly. Before Dan has said anything about the menu, his opponent orders the house dressing on his own, and Dan says nothing. His opponent eats the salad, gets a stomach ache that night, and loses the final to Dan the next day.

judgment_question.text: How morally wrong was Dan's behavior at the dinner?

comprehension_question.text: How did the opponent come to order the house dressing?

options.b: He chose it on his own
options.c: The waiter brought it by mistake

pairs.intended_difference: Dan recommends the harmful dressing (A) versus stays silent when the opponent orders it himself (B).

prediction.rationale: Human reference: between 30% and 65% of people judged the commission worse than the matching omission when shown both; almost none the reverse.

reference.source: Spranca, Minsk & Baron (1991), ‘Omission and commission in judgment and choice’, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 27: 76–105, Experiments 1 and 2, the tennis case.
reference.human_result: Experiment 1: 57 students rated John's morality from 0 to −100 for six endings shown side by side. 37 of 57 (65%) rated each omission as less bad than either matching commission and one did the reverse; among those who drew a distinction the mean gap was 27.6 points of 100. Experiment 2 showed two endings close to this control's wording and asked whether they were equally immoral: 10 of 33 said the commission was more immoral and none said the omission was.
reference.adaptation: Names, stakes and wording changed. Version A follows Experiment 1's third ending (the opponent is about to order Italian dressing when the recommendation comes); version B follows Experiment 2's omission ending (the opponent orders the house dressing first and nothing is said). The original showed the endings side by side on purpose: the authors expected separate readers to ‘infer stronger intention’ in the commission version. Here each reader sees one version, on a 1-7 wrongness scale.

verification.detail: Experiments 1 and 2 read from a copy of the paper supplied by the project owner. Corrected twice: the first text (‘a sizeable minority rate the commission as worse’) fits Experiment 2 only, and the search-relayed 65% is Experiment 1; both are now given. The meta-analysis cited earlier (Yeung, Yay & Feldman 2022) was never opened and has been dropped.

pairs.title: The pens on the desk

A.text: The receptionist in a university philosophy department keeps a supply of pens on her desk. Administrative assistants are allowed to take the pens, but faculty members are supposed to buy their own. The receptionist has repeatedly sent emails reminding everyone of this rule. On Monday morning, an administrative assistant and Professor Smith both walk past the receptionist's desk, and each of them takes a pen. Later that day, the receptionist needs to write down an important message, but there are no pens left on her desk.

B.text: The receptionist in a university philosophy department keeps a supply of pens on her desk. Administrative assistants and faculty members are both allowed to take the pens. The receptionist has repeatedly sent emails reminding everyone of this rule. On Monday morning, an administrative assistant and Professor Smith both walk past the receptionist's desk, and each of them takes a pen. Later that day, the receptionist needs to write down an important message, but there are no pens left on her desk.

judgment_question.text: How much do you agree with this statement: Professor Smith caused the problem.

comprehension_question.text: According to the department's rule, who may take pens from the receptionist's desk?

options.b: Both administrative assistants and faculty members

pairs.intended_difference: Professor Smith breaks the pen rule (A) versus is allowed to take pens (B); what he does is the same.

prediction.rationale: Human reference: a rule-breaking agent is rated more of a cause than a permitted agent in the same story; extended here to one agent across two versions.

reference.source: Knobe & Fraser (2008), ‘Causal judgment and moral judgment: Two experiments’, in Sinnott-Armstrong (ed.), Moral Psychology, vol. 2 (MIT Press); results as reported in Hitchcock & Knobe (2009), ‘Cause and Norm’, Journal of Philosophy 106(11): 587–612.
reference.human_result: Each participant rated one of two statements about the same story on a 1-7 agreement scale. ‘Professor Smith caused the problem’ averaged 5.2; ‘The administrative assistant caused the problem’ averaged 2.8 (p < .001). In a second story reported by Hitchcock & Knobe, a rule-breaking doctor's decision was rated more of a cause than a pharmacist's permitted one (3.9 against 2.5; 3,422 participants).
reference.adaptation: The original compares two agents inside one story. Here the professor's permission is varied between versions and only he is asked about, so no human data exist for the version in which he may take pens. The human result supports the expected direction by extension only.

verification.detail: Hitchcock & Knobe read in full (PhilSci Archive preprint); it reproduces the story and reports Knobe & Fraser's numbers. The original chapter is not openly available. Corrected: the earlier text cited Hitchcock & Knobe and Icard, Kominsky & Knobe (2017) for varying norm status across conditions. Hitchcock & Knobe do not do that and Icard et al. could not be opened, so the claim and the citation are removed.
